lines.speaker: Charon
lines.text: Listen, everyone. This is how it is with us. The boat's small, as you can see, and it's rotten and leaks everywhere. Tip it one way or the other and it capsizes and sinks, and here you all come at once, each of you hauling plenty of baggage. Board with all that and I'm afraid you'll regret it later — especially if you can't swim.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: So how do we sail without sinking?

lines.speaker: Charon
lines.text: I'll tell you. Board naked. Leave all this extra stuff on the shore. Even then the ferry can barely take you. Hermes, from now on don't let anyone aboard unless they're stripped bare and have ditched their gear, like I said. Stand by the gangplank, check them, and force them to board naked.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Good idea. Let's do it that way. — Who's this first one?

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Menippus. That's me. But here, Hermes, throw my bag and staff into the lake. I didn't even bring the cloak — smart move on my part.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Board, Menippus, best of men. Take the seat of honor by the steersman, up high, so you can watch everyone. And who's this handsome fellow?

lines.speaker: Charon
lines.text: Charmoleus of Megara, the lovable one whose kiss was worth two talents.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: So shed the beauty and the lips with their kisses and the thick hair and the blush on the cheeks and the whole skin. There. You're light now. Board.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: And this one in the purple robe and the diadem, the grim-looking fellow — who are you?

lines.speaker: Lampicus
lines.text: Lampicus, tyrant of Gela.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: So why come with all that baggage, Lampicus?

lines.speaker: Lampicus
lines.text: Why? Was a tyrant supposed to show up naked, Hermes?

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Not a tyrant, no. But very much a corpse. So drop it all.

lines.speaker: Lampicus
lines.text: There. The wealth's thrown away.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: And drop the arrogance, Lampicus, and the pride. It'll weigh down the ferry if it comes aboard.

lines.speaker: Lampicus
lines.text: All right, let me keep the diadem and the cloak.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: No. Drop those too.

lines.speaker: Lampicus
lines.text: Fine. What else? I've dropped everything, as you see.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: And the cruelty and the folly and the insolence and the rage. Drop those as well.

lines.speaker: Lampicus
lines.text: There. I'm stripped.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Board. Now you, the fat one, the fleshy one — who are you?

lines.speaker: Damasias
lines.text: Damasias the athlete.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Yes, you look it. I know you from seeing you in the wrestling schools often enough.

lines.speaker: Damasias
lines.text: Yes, Hermes. But take me as I am, naked.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Not naked, my friend, not with all that flesh on you. Shed it, or you'll swamp the boat stepping in with one foot. And throw away these crowns and the victory announcements too.

lines.speaker: Damasias
lines.text: There. As you see, I'm truly naked now and equal in weight to the other corpses.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Much better to be light. Board. And you, Craton, drop the wealth and the softness and the luxury. Don't bring the grave goods or the ancestral honors either. Leave behind your family, your reputation, any proclamations the city made for you, the inscriptions on your statues. And don't mention the grand tomb they built for you. All that weighs heavy when remembered.

lines.speaker: Craton
lines.text: Not willingly, but I'll throw it away. What else can I do?

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Good. Now you with the armor — what do you want? Why are you carrying that trophy?

lines.speaker: General
lines.text: Because I won, Hermes. I was the best and the city honored me.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Leave the trophy on earth. In Hades there's peace. No need for weapons.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: And this solemn one, from the look of him — all puffed up, eyebrows raised, lost in his thoughts, with that long beard hanging down. Who is he?

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: A philosopher, Hermes. Or rather a charlatan full of wonders. Strip him too. You'll see plenty of funny things hidden under that cloak.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: First drop the demeanor. Then all the rest. Zeus, what arrogance he carries. What ignorance, what strife, what vainglory, unanswerable questions, thorny arguments, convoluted thoughts. And a great deal of useless effort, no small amount of nonsense and twaddle and pettiness. And by Zeus, this gold, and pleasure-seeking, shamelessness, anger, luxury, softness. It hasn't escaped me, even if you're hiding it all well. And drop the lies, the arrogance, the idea you're better than everyone else. If you board with all that, what fifty-oared ship would take you?

lines.speaker: Philosopher
lines.text: So I drop them, since you order it.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: And let him drop this beard, Hermes. It's heavy and shaggy, as you see. At least five minas of hair.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Good point. Drop it.

lines.speaker: Philosopher
lines.text: And who's going to cut it off?

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Menippus here. He'll take a shipwright's axe and chop it off, using the gangplank as a block.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: No, Hermes, hand me a saw. That's funnier.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: The axe will do. Good. You look more human now, without that filth of yours.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Want me to take a bit off the eyebrows too?

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Absolutely. He's got them raised above his forehead, lifting himself up for some reason. What's this? Crying, you scum? Afraid to die? Board anyway.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: He still has one heaviest thing tucked under his arm.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: What is it, Menippus?

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Flattery, Hermes. It served him well in life.

lines.speaker: Philosopher
lines.text: Then you drop your freedom and your frankness and your freedom from pain and your nobility and your laughter, Menippus. You're the only one laughing here.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: No. Keep those. They're light, easy to carry, and useful for the crossing.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: And you, the rhetorician, drop all that endless verbiage, the antitheses, the parallelisms, the periods, the barbarisms, and the rest of the burdens of speech.

lines.speaker: Rhetorician
lines.text: There. I'm dropping them.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Good. So cast off the lines, take up the gangplank, haul the anchor, spread the sail, ferryman, mind the rudder. Let's sail.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Why the wailing, you fools? Especially you, philosopher, now that your beard's gone?

lines.speaker: Philosopher
lines.text: Because, Hermes, I thought the soul was immortal.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: He's lying. Something else is bothering him.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: What?

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: That he won't get to eat lavish dinners anymore, or go out at night hiding his head in his cloak, sneaking around the brothels. Or in the morning cheat the young men with his wisdom and take their silver. That's what's bothering him.

lines.speaker: Philosopher
lines.text: And you, Menippus, aren't you upset that you're dead?

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: How could I be? I hurried toward death without anyone even inviting me.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: But while we're talking — isn't that shouting I hear, like people calling from earth?

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: Yes, Menippus. Not from one place. Some are gathered in the assembly, all laughing gladly at Lampicus's death. His wife is being mobbed by the women, and the newborn children are being pelted with stones by the boys too. Others in Sicyon are praising Diophantus the rhetor as he delivers the funeral oration over this Craton here. And by Zeus, Damasias's mother is leading the lament with the women over Damasias. But you, Menippus, no one weeps for you. You lie alone in peace.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Not quite. You'll hear the dogs howling most pitifully over me, and the crows beating their wings, when they gather to bury me.

lines.speaker: Hermes
lines.text: You're a good man, Menippus. But since we've landed, you all go straight to the court that way. The ferryman and I will go fetch the others.

lines.speaker: Menippus
lines.text: Fair sailing, Hermes. Let's go then. Why are you all still hesitating? We have to be judged anyway, and they say the sentences are heavy — wheels, stones, vultures. And each man's life will be laid out in detail.
